title: Bits: All Subsets by Counting Bitmasks
oneLiner: Every number from 0 to 2^n - 1 is a different subset: bit i set means "take nums[i]". Count through them in order.
keyTakeaway: A bitmask is an integer used as a row of yes/no switches. With n elements, the masks 0 to (1 << n) - 1 are exactly the 2^n subsets, and (mask >> i) & 1 says whether element i is in. Two nested loops and no recursion: O(n * 2^n), the same as backtracking, and the order comes out fixed.
explanation:
Return every subset of nums (the power set) in this exact order: for mask = 0, 1, 2, ..., 2^n - 1, the subset holds nums[i] for every bit i that is set in mask, listed in index order. For [1, 2, 3] that is [[], [1], [2], [1, 2], [3], [1, 3], [2, 3], [1, 2, 3]]. Duplicate values are treated as different elements, so [4, 4] gives [[], [4], [4], [4, 4]].

Why it works: a subset is n independent yes/no choices, one per element, and an n-bit number is n independent 0/1 digits. Bit 0 (the 1s place) decides nums[0], bit 1 (the 2s place) decides nums[1], and so on. Counting from 0 to 2^n - 1 visits every combination of n bits exactly once, so it visits every subset exactly once. Mask 5 is 101 in binary: bits 0 and 2, so the subset [nums[0], nums[2]].

Code: total = 1 << n (that's 2^n; shifting 1 left by n places multiplies it by 2 n times). For each mask below total, loop i from 0 to n - 1 and include nums[i] when (mask >> i) & 1 is 1, or equivalently when (mask & (1 << i)) != 0. That's 2^n masks times n bit checks, O(n * 2^n) time, and the output itself is O(n * 2^n) in size.

C# versus Python. In C#, 1 << n on an int only works for n up to 30 (1 << 31 is negative, and the shift count is taken modulo 32, so 1 << 32 is 1 again, not 2^32); use 1L << n for a long. Python ints grow, so 1 << 40 is just a big number. In practice 2^n subsets is only feasible for n up to about 20 anyway.

Compared with backtracking (Backtracking: Generate All Subsets in the Patterns track), bitmasks need no recursion and the mask is a compact key: an int can stand for "which items are used" in a hash map or a DP table, which is how bitmask DP solves problems like the travelling salesman on small n.

The visualization lists the masks for [1, 2, 3]: one row per mask, one column per bit.

recognitionSignals: "All subsets / combinations" with n small (about 20 or fewer), where 2^n is affordable.
A state that is "which of these n items have been used": store it as an int mask (bitmask DP).
The required output order is by mask value, or the problem talks about binary representations of choices.
gotchas: Loop mask from 0 to (1 << n) - 1 inclusive; mask 0 is the empty subset and must be included.
Bit i corresponds to nums[i] with bit 0 the LOWEST bit, so mask 1 is [nums[0]], not [nums[n - 1]].
In C#, 1 << n overflows int past n = 30 and the shift count wraps at 32; use 1L << n for larger n.
confusableWith: Backtracking: Generate All Subsets (Patterns track) builds the same 2^n subsets with include/exclude recursion; its order is different and it extends more naturally to pruning.
Combinations of size k: you can filter masks by popcount == k, but backtracking that stops at size k is faster when k is small.

complexity.note: 2^n masks, each checked bit by bit (n steps). The output holds 2^n subsets averaging n / 2 elements, so it is O(n · 2^n) as well; extra space beyond the output is O(n) for the current subset.

referenceSolutions.python:
def subsets_by_mask(nums):
    n = len(nums)
    result = []
    for mask in range(1 << n):  # 0 .. 2^n - 1
        result.append([nums[i] for i in range(n) if (mask >> i) & 1])  # bit i set: take nums[i]
    return result
